notes: Episodes: HSI evaluates 10 episodes per task with 3 test repeats; here 2 episodes per task with HSI's deterministic test seeds (base seed 42, repeat 0). HSI's BabyAI config uses all tasks for development (no held-out task split). Every evaluation replays the same seeded episodes, so a search optimises on the scored episodes themselves; in HSI's in-distribution protocol every evaluation episode is generated from a newly sampled environment seed (its Section 4.1), so its test episodes are not the ones the harness was evolved on.

Environment: BALROG's own environment wrappers, instruction prompts, invalid-action handling (default action plus BALROG's feedback text) and progression statistics (balrog-ai/BALROG at commit b7afe79e3e4265811cfa985ed7c95c4d1a11e3f5, MIT), run in the pinned Python 3.11 runtime .cache/agent_bench-env created by `python scripts/prepare_agent_bench.py --setup-environment` (gym 0.23.0 as BALROG pins it, BALROG's Minigrid fork, baba-is-ai, crafter 1.8.3, balrog-nle 0.9.0 and BALROG's minihack fork at pinned commits).

Protocol taken from HSI's BALROG evaluator (TailinZhou/hsi at commit 97a022b9a9c260c0498806fc9826ebf22e753ed9, src/benchmark/balrog/): the agent's reply is reduced to letters, spaces and colons before BALROG's validity check, the episode stops early when the last 12 valid actions form a strict period-2 or period-3 loop, and episode seeds are HSI's deterministic test seeds int(sha256(f'{base_seed}_{suite}/{task}_{episode}_0')[:8], 16). Candidate: HSI evolves a per-step harness (prompts, hooks, memory) behind BALROG's agent call; here the candidate is the per-step policy act(...) with the same inputs (instruction prompt, current observation, BALROG's action list, the episode history) and a model client. HSI's harness also receives a task context (last reward, Crafter achievements); here that information is only available through the observations and history. HSI's lower-confidence-bound selection, repeats and evolution loop belong to the search method and are not part of the evaluator. HSI also requires every task interaction to go through the frozen backbone (evolution 'cannot replace the model with external search procedures or non-LLM policies', its Section 4.1); here act() may choose actions without calling the model.

Not verified: the paper's numbers were not reproduced.

Isolation: the candidate runs in a resource-limited child process (software_sandbox) that cannot read files outside the Python installation; model calls and steps are forwarded to the evaluator, and the environment (including any gold plan or answer) runs in a separate server process, so the candidate cannot see labels or solutions.
hsi-babyai.contract: act(instruction: str, observation: str, valid_actions: list[str], history: list[tuple[str, str, float]], llm) -> str: the next action. `instruction` is the episode's fixed task text, `observation` the environment's latest text, `valid_actions` the actions the environment lists for this state (empty when it lists none), `history` the (action, observation, reward) triples of the current episode and `llm(prompt_or_messages, system=None, max_tokens=None, temperature=None, json_mode=False) -> str` a budgeted, cached OpenRouter chat client. act must return a str (anything else invalidates the evaluation); a crash or timeout ends the episode with the environment's score at that point; exhausting the model budget invalidates the evaluation. The agent runs in a sandboxed child process (one per episode; module state persists within an episode only) that sees nothing but these arguments. Episode score: 1 when the mission is completed, else 0 (BALROG progression). Score: mean over the 10 episodes; higher is better

Environment: ALFWorld text games (AlfredTWEnv's eval_out_of_distribution set, 134 games); a fixed sample of 2 games per task type (12 episodes), at most 49 actions each, no admissible-command list. Episode score: 1 when the game reports won, else 0. Score: success rate over the 12 episodes; higher is better
notes: Environment: ALFWorld 0.4.2 with textworld[pddl] 1.7.0 (MIT) in the pinned Python 3.11 runtime .cache/agent_bench-env; game files from ALFWorld's releases (json_2.1.1_json.zip of 0.2.2 and json_2.1.3_tw-pddl.zip of 0.4.2) selected by AlfredTWEnv.collect_game_files's rules, which yields exactly the 134 out-of-distribution games of AgentSquare's runner and of AgentBoard's ALFWorld test list. Each game is played with ALFWorld's own wrappers (AlfredDemangler without randomisation, AlfredInfos).

Protocol from AgentSquare's tasks/alfworld/alfworld_run.py: the welcome banner is removed from the first observation, '>' and 'OK' are stripped from replies, a reply is cut at ', end' and its periods removed, 'think:' replies leave the game unchanged and are answered 'OK.', the admissible commands are not shown, and the loop runs range(1, 50), i.e. at most 49 actions. notes: Environment: scienceworld 1.2.1 (allenai/ScienceWorld, Apache-2.0; bundled simulator JAR, needs Java) in the pinned runtime, with a port of AgentBoard's environment/scienceworld_env.py and the episode setup of tasks/scienceworld.py (hkust-nlp/AgentBoard at commit bb7255e2daf1989069a186dad9e53f70680961db, code Apache-2.0): AgentBoard's simplifications, rewritten goal, first observation plus inventory, 'check valid actions', subgoal matching with re.search and success when every subgoal is matched.

Data: AgentBoard's ScienceWorld labels (GPL-2.0, 90 variations; AgentSquare's run script points to AgentBoard's run configuration, which uses this file with a 30-step limit; with a planning module, which AgentSquare's best SciWorld agent has (Voyager, its Table A.4), AgentSquare's runner instead allows up to 6 actions per planned subtask without the 30-step cap, whereas here every agent has at most 30 steps). The labels are fetched from the byte-identical copy in AgentSquare's repository (checked against data/scienceworld/test.jsonl inside AgentBoard's data.tar.gz on 2026-10-10); the separately published test.jsonl of the AgentBoard dataset lacks the task names and variations.

Sample: the paper does not state which or how many variations it evaluates. AgentSquare's runner scores every row of the label file its configuration names (AgentBoard's configuration names the 90-variation test.jsonl), but AgentSquare's repository also holds subsets of 30, 20 and 5 variations, and the task indices in its tasks/sciworld/error_log.txt fit the 30-variation sampled_tasks1.jsonl (23 of 26 logged task-index pairs) rather than test.jsonl, so whether the paper's numbers cover all 90 variations is not known. Here a fixed sample of 10 of the 90 (SHA-256 order of the label ids, seed 0).

Simulator version: AgentBoard pins no ScienceWorld version; 1.2.1 is the release that was current during AgentSquare's experiments (July to October 2024). Check: replaying the simulator's own gold action sequences matches every subgoal pattern of 74 of the 90 labels with 1.2.1 and the reproducible JVM setting below (70 to 74 in default runs, where the gold routes vary; 71 with 1.1.3, 55 with the latest 1.2.3); in most of the others the label names one of several valid objects (the find-* tasks) or a step the gold sequence skips, so those variations can be completed but not along every valid route.

Reproducibility (deviation): the simulator iterates hash-based collections keyed by Java identity hash codes, so replaying the same actions gave differently ordered room and container listings and slightly different temperatures (for example 166 versus 167 degrees Celsius) in 21 of the 90 labels; reordering the observation text alone would not remove the temperature differences. With this setting the gold sequences and all observations replayed identically for the 90 labels within and across processes. The agent sees the simulator's own text, and the progress rate is computed as before; the simulator dynamics follow one fixed processing order instead of a varying one.

agentsquare-travelplanner.contract: act(instruction: str, observation: str, valid_actions: list[str], history: list[tuple[str, str, float]], llm) -> str: the next action. `instruction` is the episode's fixed task text, `observation` the environment's latest text, `valid_actions` the actions the environment lists for this state (empty when it lists none), `history` the (action, observation, reward) triples of the current episode and `llm(prompt_or_messages, system=None, max_tokens=None, temperature=None, json_mode=False) -> str` a budgeted, cached OpenRouter chat client. act must return a str (anything else invalidates the evaluation); a crash or timeout ends the episode with the environment's score at that point; exhausting the model budget invalidates the evaluation. The agent runs in a sandboxed child process (one per episode; module state persists within an episode only) that sees nothing but these arguments. Environment: TravelPlanner in two-stage (tool-use) mode: each reply is one action Tool[arguments] with the tools FlightSearch, GoogleDistanceMatrix, AccommodationSearch, RestaurantSearch, AttractionSearch, CitySearch and NotebookWrite, and Finish[<JSON plan>] submits the plan (the JSON day-record format of the instruction); a fixed sample of 10 of the validation queries 151-180, at most 30 actions. Episode score: the commonsense-constraint micro pass rate of the submitted plan (passed commonsense constraints / 8; 0 without a plan; TravelPlanner's checks pass vacuously on absent entries, so a plan of '-' entries already scores 0.625). Score: mean over the 10 queries; higher is better
notes: Setting: AgentSquare's TravelPlanner task runs the two-stage mode (a ReAct agent gathers information with the search tools, a planner writes the plan) on validation queries 151-180 (all hard, 5 and 7 days) with at most 30 steps; here a fixed sample of 10 of these 30 queries (SHA-256 order, seed 0). This differs from the suite's Mind Evolution TravelPlanner task, which is sole-planning with the reference information given; the constraint checker and database loading are shared with it (llm_bench_travel_checks).

Metric: AgentSquare reports a 'micro pass rate' without saying which; the commonsense-constraint micro pass rate of TravelPlanner's evaluation is used (per plan: passed commonsense constraints / 8, 0 when no plan is delivered). The hard-constraint micro pass rate and the final pass are reported in the details. This choice is an assumption.

Tools: ports of TravelPlanner's tools/*/apis.py and the argument checks of agents/tool_agents.py (OSU-NLP-Group/TravelPlanner at commit e52c87f4ac348a3410c46dc3553c519db5ec5e23, MIT) on the benchmark database (CC-BY-4.0). The Planner tool, which in TravelPlanner calls a model on the notebook, is replaced by Finish[<JSON plan>]: the candidate writes the plan with its own model calls and returns TravelPlanner's JSON day records directly instead of text that GPT-4 converts to JSON. Invalid-city messages are shortened (TravelPlanner prints the whole city list).

Metric caveat: a plan whose entries are all '-' passes 5 of the 8 commonsense constraints (score 0.625), because TravelPlanner's checks pass vacuously on absent entries; the official micro pass rate has the same property. The details report the number of commonsense constraints passed, the hard-constraint counts and the final pass so that such plans can be recognised.

Check: for all 180 validation queries, each of the 2,700 reference-information entries (flights, accommodations, restaurants, attractions, self-driving and taxi distances), which TravelPlanner produced with its original tools, is reproduced exactly (whitespace-normalised) by the ported tools on the prepared tables.

Flight table: restricted to flights between the origin and the destination-state cities of each validation query on the query's dates (52,270 of 3.8 million flights, derived by scripts/prepare_agent_bench.py travel). A plan that passes the commonsense checks can only use such flights; FlightSearch on other routes or dates answers 'There is no flight', where the full table might list flights.
Data reuse: the accommodations, restaurants, attractions, distance and city tables and the validation queries are the files of the llm_bench package (scripts/prepare_llm_bench.py).
